title: Nehemiah 9:16–25
context: The prayer turns to Israel’s rebellion: the fathers acted proudly, hardened their necks, forgot God’s wonders, appointed a leader to return to bondage (compare Numbers 14:4), and made the molded calf. Yet God, ready to pardon, gracious and merciful, slow to anger, and abundant in loving kindness (compare Exodus 34:6), did not forsake them, kept leading them by cloud and fire, gave his good Spirit to instruct them, sustained them forty years, and gave them kingdoms, a multiplied people, and a rich land full of good things. The section ends with the people eating, being filled, growing fat, and delighting in God’s great goodness, words that echo the warnings of Deuteronomy (compare Deuteronomy 6:11; 32:15). Arminian and Reformed readers commonly read the passage as shared ground about God’s patient mercy in the face of persistent sin. They describe differently how God’s faithfulness to his people relates to the response of each generation, but the prayer itself stresses the mercy all readers confess.

verses.text: “But they and our fathers behaved proudly, hardened their neck, didn’t listen to your commandments,
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the fathers acting proudly, hardening their necks, and refusing to listen. Rebellion is a real and responsible choice.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the hardened neck as revealing the depth of human sin. Both traditions commonly read the verse as honest confession of the people’s history (compare Psalm 95:8).

verses.text: and refused to obey. They weren’t mindful of your wonders that you did among them, but hardened their neck, and in their rebellion appointed a captain to return to their bondage. But you are a God ready to pardon, gracious and merciful, slow to anger, and abundant in loving kindness, and didn’t forsake them.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the people forgetting God’s wonders and choosing a leader to return to bondage, yet God remaining ready to pardon. Mercy meets rebellion.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the confession of God’s character echoing Exodus 34:6. Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse as shared ground about God’s patient grace.

verses.text: Yes, when they had made themselves a molded calf, and said, ‘This is your God who brought you up out of Egypt,’ and had committed awful blasphemies,
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the people making the molded calf and calling it the god who brought them from Egypt. Their sin is grievous.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the calf as the classic example of idolatry within the covenant people (compare Exodus 32:4). Both traditions commonly read the verse as a sobering confession.

verses.text: yet you in your manifold mercies didn’t forsake them in the wilderness. The pillar of cloud didn’t depart from over them by day, to lead them in the way; neither did the pillar of fire by night, to show them light, and the way in which they should go.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see God, in his manifold mercies, not forsaking the people and keeping the pillar of cloud and fire. Mercy continues despite sin.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God’s faithfulness as greater than the people’s unfaithfulness. Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse as praise for God’s steadfast love.

verses.text: You gave also your good Spirit to instruct them, and didn’t withhold your manna from their mouth, and gave them water for their thirst.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see God giving his good Spirit to instruct the people, along with manna and water. They commonly see the Spirit’s instruction as gracious help that the people could heed or neglect.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the good Spirit as God’s own presence teaching his people (compare Isaiah 63:11; Psalm 143:10). Both traditions commonly read the verse as shared ground about God’s generous care.

verses.text: “Yes, forty years you sustained them in the wilderness. They lacked nothing. Their clothes didn’t grow old, and their feet didn’t swell.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see God sustaining the people forty years so that they lacked nothing. Even their clothes and feet were preserved.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see detailed providence in the wilderness (compare Deuteronomy 8:4). Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse as assurance of God’s faithful provision.

verses.text: Moreover you gave them kingdoms and peoples, which you allotted according to their portions. So they possessed the land of Sihon, even the land of the king of Heshbon, and the land of Og king of Bashan.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see God giving the people kingdoms, including the lands of Sihon and Og. God fulfills his promises step by step.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the victories as God’s gift rather than Israel’s achievement. Both traditions commonly read the verse as praise for God’s faithfulness.

verses.text: You also multiplied their children as the stars of the sky, and brought them into the land concerning which you said to their fathers that they should go in to possess it.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see God multiplying the children like the stars and bringing them into the land. The promise to Abraham is kept.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the fulfillment of God’s word to the fathers (compare Genesis 15:5). Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse as evidence of God’s reliability.

verses.text: “So the children went in and possessed the land; and you subdued before them the inhabitants of the land, the Canaanites, and gave them into their hands, with their kings and the peoples of the land, that they might do with them as they pleased.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the children possessing the land as God subdued its inhabitants. The conquest is described as God’s gift.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God’s sovereign action in giving the land. Both traditions commonly read the verse within Israel’s particular history, without turning it into a general pattern.

verses.text: They took fortified cities and a rich land, and possessed houses full of all good things, cisterns dug out, vineyards, olive groves, and fruit trees in abundance. So they ate, were filled, became fat, and delighted themselves in your great goodness.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the people taking cities, houses full of good things, and fruitful land, and delighting in God’s goodness. Abundance can be a blessing or a temptation.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the language of growing fat as an echo of warnings against forgetting God (compare Deuteronomy 32:15). Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse as preparing for the confession of later rebellion.
